query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a 5–10 μm silicide- or aluminide-based oxidation-resistant coating on as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will impede oxygen diffusion at ~1000 °C in air for at least 100 hours without degrading the alloy’s high-temperature strength (163–530 MPa) or usable ductility (8–16%).
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, exhibiting ~8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C (strain rates 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹)
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin (5–10 μm) silicide- or aluminide-based surface coating via pack cementation or chemical vapor deposition
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 1000 °C for up to 100 hours under tensile load (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹)
generation.structural_mediator: Engineered coating forms stable oxide (e.g., SiO₂ or Al₂O₃) that impedes inward oxygen transport
generation.mechanism: By creating a dense, protective scale, oxygen infiltration is limited, mitigating phase destabilization and embrittlement in the substrate, thereby maintaining the alloy’s inherent mechanical integrity at high temperature
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated specimens retain comparable yield strength (163–530 MPa) and tensile ductility (≥8% at room temperature) relative to baseline in inert environments, with minimal oxide scale formation on the substrate
generation.baseline: Uncoated as-cast HfNbTaTiZr suffers increased oxidation and embrittlement, leading to reduced strength and ductility with prolonged oxygen exposure at 1000 °C
generation.boundary: If the coating is excessively thin (<5 μm), localized spallation or cracking may occur; if it is too thick or poorly bonded, thermal mismatch can induce spalling or stress risers that compromise ductility
generation.uncertainty: Potential mismatch in thermal expansion, coating-substrate compatibility, or brittleness of oxide scales may lower strain tolerance in service

falsification_experiment.design: Apply identical thermal (1000 °C in air, 100 h) and tensile (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) loading to paired sets of coated and uncoated HfNbTaTiZr coupons to compare oxidation kinetics and mechanical performance post-exposure
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and composition (via SEM/EDS or XRD)
Tensile strength and ductility at 1000 °C post-exposure
Fractography to assess oxide-related failure modes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples exhibit oxygen uptake and mechanical degradation similar to uncoated controls, the hypothesis is falsified. If they maintain strength and ductility values near untreated baseline levels, and exhibit reduced oxygen ingress, the hypothesis is supported.

cited_evidence.text: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. decision.trend: Among the published work focusing on HfNbTaTiZr-based refractory high-entropy alloys, PMC7514121 examines a subtraction approach (including HfNbTaTiZr) to reveal how each constituent element affects mechanical properties, emphasizing compressive strength but not oxidation resistance. PMC7514597 studies the room-temperature tensile properties of HfNbTaTiZr and derivatives, highlighting the beneficial role of a BCC phase fraction for ductility but leaving oxidation issues unaddressed. PMC10453588 investigates a closely related NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy’s high-temperature deformation mechanisms and demonstrates robust strength at 673–873 K, again without offering an explicit solution for oxygen-induced degradation. Overall, the community has focused on mechanical and microstructural optimization, but the challenge of mitigating high-temperature oxygen attack remains largely unsolved.
decision.unsolved: No prior publication in this set targets how to protect as-cast HfNbTaTiZr from oxygen infiltration at 1000 °C while maintaining its ductility (8–16%) and strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C). The missing link is a strategy that blocks or reduces oxidation without negatively altering the alloy’s notable mechanical performance.
decision.lever: Deposit a thin (5–10 μm) oxidation-resistant coating—such as a silicide-based or aluminide layer (for instance, via pack cementation or chemical vapor deposition)—capable of forming a stable protective scale (e.g., SiO2 or Al2O3) in high-temperature applications. The hypothesis is that this barrier layer will impede oxygen diffusion at ~1000 °C for at least 100 hours of air exposure at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹, preserving the underlying alloy’s strength and ductility relative to untreated HfNbTaTiZr. Prior success with protective coatings on other refractory alloys supports this approach. A controlled falsification experiment would involve comparing uncoated and coated samples under identical high-temperature oxygen-rich conditions and mechanical loading to confirm reductions in oxide scale formation and preservation of mechanical properties.
